findings.summary: A "Next page" pointer promises `git bisect run` on the following page, but the exit-code mechanism it points to is on the same page directly beneath it.
findings.evidence: Page 5: callout "Next page" — "`git bisect run <cmd>` does the whole loop for you — exit codes decide {green:good} / {red:bad} / {orange:skip}." is immediately followed on the same slide by heading "1. Mechanism: exit codes" and the 0 / 1-124 / 125 / 128+ table.
findings.fix: Retitle the callout to a plain bridge (e.g. "Automating the loop") with no page reference, or drop it since the exit-code table follows immediately.

findings.summary: The automated-bisect chapter summary appears on page 7 after page 6 has already opened the reflog chapter, so the bisect wrap-up interrupts the reflog teaching sequence.
findings.evidence: Page 6 ends with "1. What Reflog Is" / "==git reflog== (short for `git reflog show HEAD`) lists __every position HEAD has held__"; page 7 then opens with "5. Summary" / "0 good · 1-127 bad · **125 skip** — the whole contract." before the `$ git reflog` example.
findings.fix: Move the "5. Summary" checkbox block (bisect exit-code contract) to the end of page 6, immediately before the "1. What Reflog Is" heading, so the reflog chapter opens uninterrupted on page 7.

findings.summary: `git reflog expire --all` without an explicit `--expire` does not wipe the reflog, so it is not equivalent to the destructive `gc --prune=now` claim it is paired with.
findings.evidence: "`git reflog expire --all` = same damage, quieter" (page 10, "3. Reflog Mistakes"), versus page 8's own correct form: "`git reflog expire --expire=now --all` **destroys** the safety net". git-reflog(1): "If this option is not specified, the expiration time is taken from the configuration setting `gc.reflogExpire`, which in turn defaults to 90 days" (and 30 days for unreachable).
findings.fix: Change the bullet to `git reflog expire --expire=now --all` = same damage, quieter — and note that bare `git reflog expire --all` only applies the 90/30-day defaults, deleting almost nothing.

findings.summary: The decorative pushpin graphic anchoring each yellow sticky note is drawn on top of the last code line of the block behind it, partially occluding characters in copyable commands.
findings.evidence: Page 3, line 3 of the first code block reads `git push origin release-1.4` with the pin head covering the `.4`; page 6, reflog block line `1a2b3c4 HEAD@{3}: checkout: to feat` has the pin over `checkout:`; page 8, `# or: git reset --hard a1b2c3d` has the pin over the tail of the SHA `a1b2c3d`; page 5, `git bisect slow; git bisect fast` has the pin between `bisect` and `fast`.
findings.fix: Offset the sticky-note pin so it anchors outside the code block's text column (e.g. pin at the note's top-right, or shift the note down by one line-height) so no pin overlaps a rendered code glyph.

findings.summary: Two page subtitles are stale copies that mislabel what the page teaches.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ("Revert, Duplicates and Bisect Setup") carries subtitle "Which tool, when" copied from page 3; page 10 ("Reflog Traps, Trade-offs and Flag Recap") carries subtitle "Where these tools bite" copied from page 9.
findings.fix: Set page 4's subtitle to something like "Revert, then start bisect" and page 10's to "Cheatsheet".

findings.summary: The three-tools table classifies each command by "Touches: patch / history / pointers" before the patch-vs-pointer-vs-history model is explained on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 table rows "I want this change here | cherry-pick | patch", "Which change broke it | bisect | history", "Where did my commit go | reflog | pointers"; the defining callout "Three layers: ==patches== (content diffs, cherry-pick) vs ==pointers== (refs, reflog) vs ==history== (the DAG, bisect)" only appears on page 2.
findings.fix: Move the "Mental model for the book" callout onto page 1 immediately before the three-tools table, so the Touches column is read against a definition.

findings.summary: `patch-id` is used as the explanation for what `git cherry` matches on, one page before patch-id is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 2 code note: "read-only scout, patch-id matched"; the definition arrives on page 3 — "`rebase` and `git cherry` match by ==patch-id==, not SHA".
findings.fix: Expand the page 2 note to define it in place, e.g. "read-only scout — matches by patch content (patch-id), not SHA".

findings.summary: The `HEAD@{n}` reflog selector is used to show how an orphaned commit is recovered five pages before the `@{n}` syntax is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 2 chain diagram step: "reflog entry keeps it alive" / note "HEAD@{1} finds it"; the selector is only explained on page 7 — "`HEAD@{2}` | **2 moves** ago" and "`@{n}` walks the __journal__; `~n` walks __parents__".
findings.fix: On page 2, write the note in prose ("the previous HEAD position still names it") and defer the `HEAD@{1}` notation to page 7, or add a half-line gloss: "HEAD@{1} = HEAD's previous position (page 7)".

findings.summary: Claims a whitespace-only difference defeats patch-id matching, but Git's patch-id ignores whitespace by default.
findings.evidence: "One edited line, one whitespace fix = ==no match==" (page 3, section 3). git-patch-id(1), `--stable`/`--unstable` (the default): "All whitespace within the patch is ignored and does not affect the ID"; only `--verbatim` (or `patchid.verbatim=true`) preserves whitespace.
findings.fix: Drop the whitespace example: "One edited line, one rebased context change = no match (whitespace-only differences still match — patch-id ignores whitespace unless `patchid.verbatim` is set)."

findings.summary: A forward reference tells the reader that page 3 covers the duplicate-patch cost, but the callout is itself on page 3 and the cost material runs on into page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 3 callout "Copy, not move": "The source commit is untouched; the patch now exists **twice** under two SHAs. Page 3 covers what that costs you."
findings.fix: Change the sentence to point at the correct location — "The next section, and the trade-off table on page 4, cover what that costs you."

findings.summary: Attributes patch-id deduplication to `git merge`, which never consults patch-ids, and states a byte-identical requirement that does not hold.
findings.evidence: Note on the "Duplicate Commit" example (`git cherry-pick abc` then `git merge feat`): "patch-id drops it only if byte-identical". patch-id is used by rebase / `git cherry` / `format-patch`, not by merge; merge resolves an identical change on both sides through the three-way content merge, and patch-id itself ignores whitespace rather than requiring byte identity.
findings.fix: Replace the note with "merge doesn't use patch-id at all — identical content merges cleanly, any edit to the picked copy conflicts".

findings.summary: The fuzzy-result tip prescribes `--term-old` as a remedy for untestable commits, which contradicts the definition given on page 5 where the flag only renames the good/bad verdicts.
findings.evidence: Page 6 tip "Reading a fuzzy result": "Several candidates listed = fix the untestable commits (patch the build, `--term-old`) and replay with `git bisect replay b.log`." versus page 5: "`--term-old=fast --term-new=slow` renames the verdicts".
findings.fix: Replace `--term-old` in the tip with the action that actually reduces skips — e.g. "patch the build inside the probe, or return 125 only for genuinely untestable commits" — and then replay.

findings.summary: Says dropped stash entries live under `refs/stash`, but dropping a stash removes its entry from that ref's reflog.
findings.evidence: "Dropped stash: entries live under `refs/stash`" followed by "Truly orphaned stash: `git fsck --unreachable`". `git stash drop` deletes the `stash@{n}` reflog entry from `refs/stash`; recovering a dropped stash is exactly the fsck case.
findings.fix: Reword to "Live stash entries: `refs/stash` + its reflog (`git stash list`); **dropped** stash: gone from `refs/stash`, recover via `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit`."

findings.summary: Points readers at the reflog of a bare server-side repository without noting that bare repos keep no reflog by default.
findings.evidence: "Server-side: only your own host's `git reflog` on the bare repo helps". `core.logAllRefUpdates` is enabled by default only for repositories with a working tree, so a bare repo logs no ref updates unless `git config core.logAllRefUpdates true` was set (hosting providers such as GitHub enable their own equivalent).
findings.fix: Add the caveat: "...and only if that bare repo has `core.logAllRefUpdates=true` — bare repos keep no reflog by default."

findings.summary: The "Four More Playbooks" heading does not match the five-row table beneath it.
findings.evidence: Heading "2. Four More Playbooks" over a table with rows: "Force-pushed over colleague", "Deleted merged branch", "Rebase sideways, mid-run", "Rebase already finished", "Picked onto wrong branch" — five entries.
findings.fix: Retitle to "2. Five More Playbooks" (or drop the count: "2. More Playbooks").

findings.summary: `git gc --prune=now` does not by itself destroy the recovery window, because gc explicitly keeps objects still referenced by reflog entries.
findings.evidence: "`git gc --prune=now` destroys the recovery window" (page 10). git-gc(1): gc "will keep not only objects referenced by your current set of branches and tags, but also objects referenced by the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs ... and anything else in the refs/* namespace"; reflog entries themselves only expire at gc.reflogExpire (90 days) / gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (30 days). Page 8 states this correctly: "only run it right before a genuine `gc --prune=now`".
findings.fix: Reword to "`git gc --prune=now` drops unreachable objects immediately — but only those the reflog no longer references; it becomes fatal once the reflog has been expired."
